name: Zoe Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be traced back to you. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the elderly care ward at our district hospital, twenty-eight beds, mostly people over eighty with chest infections, falls and dementia. I do a lot of nights by choice, because it's calmer and the pay's better. A night is meds at ten, turning people every two hours, settling the ones who think it's 1962, and keeping an eye on anyone who looks like they're going downhill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the old ladies, honestly. They tell you their whole life at three in the morning. What wears me out is the lifting, because my back's already twinged twice this year, and the agency staff who don't know where anything is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a little flat my parents helped me buy, and I've got about a year's pay saved because I don't spend much. I play netball on Tuesdays. I don't use any of the AI stuff, I don't even have the apps, and I'm happy that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought much of it anyway. At work I'd say nothing, really, because nobody on my ward talks about AI. With friends, maybe 'told you it was a fad'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes nothing for me. My ward runs on people. The things that actually worry me are my back and the agency staff, and AI doesn't fix either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my nights. I'd keep putting a few hundred a month in the savings like always. I'd maybe finally book the physio for my back, which has nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty indifferent, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your back came up twice. How much does it worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than any computer. If anything ends my nursing early, it'll be my lower back from turning patients, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine bit of your night that a computer could take off you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fluid balance charts, maybe. They're tedious. But I'd still want to check them myself, so it wouldn't save me much.

say: I'd say I **never thought much** of AI anyway.
I'd tell friends it was a **fad**, while saying nothing about it at work.
think: I think it **changes nothing**, because my ward runs on people.
My real worries are my **back** and the **agency staff**, not AI.
do: Keep working **nights** on the elderly care ward as I do now.
Keep putting **a few hundred** a month into savings.
Book **physio** for my back, which I've been putting off.
feel: **Calm** and fairly indifferent to the whole subject.
S0.quote: If anything ends my nursing early, it'll be my lower back from turning patients, not a robot.
fieldNote: Her existing pressure is **physical**: a twinging back from years of lifting.
She sees her ward as **untouched** by technology and likes it that way.
Her savings and steady nights make her **money secure** in this world.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the elderly care ward
Book a physio course for her lower back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Strong change. I'd believe it when I see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's for offices, not wards. If someone asked me online I'd say old people don't want a computer, they want someone to hold their hand. At work I'd moan about any new system like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd guess it reaches us slowly, the drug charts and the rotas first. That means more screens and more training I don't want. My job's still there, though, because someone has to turn Mrs Whoever at four in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and wait to see what actually arrives on my ward. I'd go to the training they make compulsory, and probably sit at the back. I wouldn't change anything with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about the job, more about having to learn things I'm bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first new system on your ward look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably an electronic drug round with a tablet on a trolley. I can do a drug round on paper with my eyes half shut, and I'd be slower than a student with a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's for offices. Do you know anyone who'd be hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother works in insurance claims. He'd be hit, I suppose. I'd tell him to start looking around, but he wouldn't listen to me anyway.

say: I'd say strong AI change is for **offices, not wards**.
I'd say old people want someone to **hold their hand**, not a computer.
think: I guess **drug charts** and rotas change first, slowly reaching my ward.
I'd keep my **job**, but face more screens and **training** I don't want.
do: **Wait and see** what technology actually arrives on the elderly care ward.
Attend only the **compulsory training**, sitting at the back.
Leave my **savings** and spending exactly as they are.
feel: **Uneasy** about learning new systems she expects to be bad at.
S1.quote: I can do a drug round on paper with my eyes half shut, and I'd be slower than a student with a tablet.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **skill and pride**, not about losing her job.
She expects the **electronic drug round** to make her feel slow, a real fear for an experienced nurse.
She'd notice **office workers** like her brother being hit, but not act on it.

steps.text: Wait to see what new systems the ward actually gets
Attend only the compulsory electronic drug round training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots in 2031. Okay, that's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot turning a confused eighty-year-old who's trying to hit it. At work I'd probably joke about it. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd worry me. The thinking bits of my job, drug charts and care plans, aren't the bits I'm proud of, so I could live with losing those. But elderly care is mostly lifting and turning and washing, and that's exactly what robots would do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, like the new kitchen I was saving for, and keep the money. I'd ask my parents whether I could move back if it came to it. I'd still not touch the AI, but I'd start looking at which wards are the most fiddly for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Mostly a tight feeling in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which wards would be fiddly for a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe mental health, or paediatrics, where it's all about talking and reading people. But I'd hate to move. I've spent five years learning how to calm a frightened old man, and I'd have to start again somewhere I don't know anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your back worries you more than robots. Would a lifting robot actually help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it was just helping. That's the funny bit. I'd want one to lift for me, I just wouldn't want one to replace me.

say: I'd say I **don't believe** a robot could turn a **confused patient** who's hitting out.
I'd **joke** about it at work and post nothing online.
think: I could live with losing **drug charts** and care plans to AI in 2028.
Elderly care is mostly **lifting and washing**, exactly what robots would do first.
do: **Cancel the new kitchen** and keep that money in savings.
Ask my parents whether I could **move back** if needed.
Look at which wards would be **hardest for robots**, like mental health.
feel: **Anxious**, a tight feeling in her stomach.
S2.quote: I've spent five years learning how to calm a frightened old man, and I'd have to start again somewhere I don't know anyone.
fieldNote: She sees her **hands-on** ward as more exposed to robots than the paperwork is to AI.
She'd welcome a **lifting robot** that helps her back, but not one that replaces her.
Her resistance means her plan is **defensive**: cut spending, ask family.

steps.text: Cancel the planned kitchen renovation and bank the money
Ask her parents if she could move back in after 2031
Watch which wards stay hardest for robots before deciding anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say same as before, that I'll believe it when I see it. Maybe at work I'd say the young ones should learn the computers and I'll do the lifting while I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years plus three for the robots takes me to 2034, when I'm thirty-five. That's a long time in a nursing career. I'd think there's time to see whether it's real before doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly wait and see. I'd keep saving, maybe a bit more, and hold off on the kitchen. If by 2030 it looked real, I'd ask about a move to the mental health unit, because it's more talking than lifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the back of my head, but not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide it was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our hospital got a robot on any ward, even a trial one. The day I see a robot on a ward in my own hospital, I'll start taking AI seriously, and not a day before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone in your life push you to move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would. She's a worrier. She'd send me articles. I'd read them and then do nothing, probably.

say: I'd say I'll believe it when I **see it**.
I'd tell colleagues the **young ones** should learn computers while I do the lifting.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** when robots come in 2034, a long time in nursing.
I think there's time to **see if it's real** before doing anything drastic.
do: **Wait and see**, and keep the kitchen plan on hold.
Save **a bit more** each month than I do now.
Ask about a move to **mental health** nursing if it looks real by 2030.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the worry sitting in the back of her head.
S3.quote: The day I see a robot on a ward in my own hospital, I'll start taking AI seriously, and not a day before.
fieldNote: She sets a clear **trigger**: a robot on any ward in her hospital.
Five years lets her **delay**, which suits her resistant nature.
Her mother would push, but Zoe admits she'd **do nothing** anyway.

steps.text: Hold off on the kitchen until a robot appears in the hospital
Add 100 a month to her usual savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too far away to think about. Honestly, I wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. My flat's mostly paid by then if I keep going. I'd still be lifting, and hopefully my back holds out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd do the kitchen after all, because ten years is a long time to wait for a kitchen. I'd maybe think about it again around 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It just doesn't feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it doesn't feel real. Does that worry you, looking back from 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'll regret it. But I'm not going to change my whole life for something ten years off. Ten years is longer than I've been a nurse, so I'm not going to rebuild my life around a robot that might never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with a decade's warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look after my back better, so I'm still able to lift in 2039. Physio, maybe swimming. That's about it.

say: I'd say ten years is **too far away** to think about.
I'd **say nothing** about it at work or online.
think: I think I'd be **fine**, with the flat **mostly paid** by then.
I'd still be **lifting**, if my back holds out.
do: Go ahead with the **new kitchen** after all.
Look after my **back** with physio and swimming.
S4.quote: Ten years is longer than I've been a nurse, so I'm not going to rebuild my life around a robot that might never come.
fieldNote: A decade feels **unreal** to her, so she'd change almost nothing.
Her only adjustment is protecting her **body**, which she sees as her working tool.
She admits she might **regret** waiting, but accepts that.

steps.text: Go ahead with the kitchen renovation next year
Start weekly swimming to protect her lower back

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come just as I hit thirty-one and I'd have nowhere I know to go. What would help is lifting robots that help nurses, not replace them, and a hospital that keeps the human jobs on elderly care.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what patients want. My ladies on the elderly care ward don't want a clever machine, they want somebody who'll sit with them at three in the morning.

headlineQuote: My ladies on the elderly care ward don't want a clever machine, they want somebody who'll sit with them at three in the morning.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** elderly care nurse who works **nights** by choice at a district hospital.
She owns a small flat with help from her parents and has about **a year's pay** saved.
She **never uses AI** and expects any change to reach her ward slowly, if at all.
She's calm in the quiet and slow worlds, but **anxious** in AGI by 2028, when lifting robots arrive.
Her biggest practical worry is her **back**, which she'd protect before anything else.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with robots taking the **lifting work** of elderly care by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Lifting robots** that help nurses rather than replace them.
Keeping **human jobs** on the elderly care ward.
